We build with real data and measurable results. Our team is complete, but we're always happy to connect and share ideas with the Space Apps community.
summary: SERENA (Sensor Evidence and Reliability Engine for Next-frontier Astronauts) is a health-monitoring system for long-duration missions, where a response from Earth can take up to 20 minutes to arrive. SERENA does not replace health monitoring from Earth. It is an onboard complement to it, for the moments when the crew cannot wait for an answer from mission control. Its main feature is that it checks whether each sensor reading can be trusted before using it. On the way to the Moon or Mars, astronauts often have to make health decisions on their own, and NASA's own reports show that wearable sensors lose data, pick up motion noise and drift over time. Acting on a wrong reading can be as dangerous as missing a real event. SERENA adds a deterministic verification step, which we call Layer 0, that checks the source and integrity of each reading, whether it is current, its signal quality, whether different sensors agree, and how it compares with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline. Only after that does it show the value and guide the crew on what to do. Everything runs offline, and the communication delay to Earth is always visible.
details:
Links

Live app: https://serena-demo.onrender.com/#station

Source code: https://github.com/Barbarasanchez11/SERENA

What SERENA is

SERENA is health-monitoring software for astronauts on long-duration missions, where a response from Earth can take up to 20 minutes to arrive and the crew often has to decide alone. It collects health indicators, helps the crew assess their own health and suggests what to do next. It is not meant to compete with or replace the medical monitoring done from Earth by flight surgeons and mission control. It is an additional onboard layer for long-duration missions, so the crew has reliable information while they wait for a reply, or when there is no link at all. What makes it different is a verification layer that decides whether each reading can be trusted before it is interpreted. If the data cannot be verified, SERENA says so instead of presenting it as a normal result.

The problem

The challenge asks for software that helps astronauts assess and act on their own health. Two things make this hard far from Earth. The first is distance: a round trip to Mars can take up to about 40 minutes and the link is not always available, so the crew often has to decide alone. The second is sensor reliability: NASA technical reports describe heart-rate monitors losing data and picking up motion artefact in flight, and body-worn inertial sensors slipping, switching off early and being hard to synchronise. A corrupted reading can look exactly like a correct one. Acting on a wrong value can be as dangerous as missing a real emergency, so we treat data reliability as a safety problem in itself.

How it works: Layer 0

Before a value is shown as something the astronaut can act on, it goes through five deterministic checks:

  1. Source and integrity: a cryptographic signature confirms the reading comes from that sensor and has not been altered.
  2. Timeliness: old or replayed values cannot pass as live data.
  3. Signal quality: the waveform has to be clean enough to read, not dominated by motion or noise.
  4. Sensor agreement: different sensors must be consistent with each other (for example, a pulse should follow each heartbeat). These rules are written in signal temporal logic.
  5. Personal baseline: the value is compared with the astronaut's own pre-flight normal, not a population average.

A reading is marked VERIFIED only if it passes all of them. Manual entries (blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, radiation dose) are also checked for plausible ranges, consistency with sensor data and suspicious repetition.

How the astronaut reads the data

Each value is shown on two separate axes, always with a text label and never with colour alone:

  • Colour shows health status: green, amber, red or unknown.
  • Fill shows data confidence: solid means verified and safe to act on, hatched means it could not be verified.

If a value is within the normal range but cannot be verified, it is shown as Unknown. We did not want an unverified "normal" number to reassure anyone.

The crew workflow

SERENA covers the whole cycle: collect, verify, evaluate, act and record. The interface follows the same order a person would: Feel (the astronaut reports symptoms), Measure (latest sensor readings with their status), Trust (the result of the five checks) and Act (an action card with clear instructions). Each action card has an escalation level: 1) act on your own, 2) notify the crew, 3) contact flight surgeons on Earth. Level 3 shows the real round-trip delay for the current location (ISS about 0 s, Moon about 1.3 s, Mars 3 to 22 min). There is also a "no communication" mode for solar conjunction, which disables level 3.

The interface

The app runs inside a 3D spaceship with four environments (Command Bridge, Space Station, Lunar Base and Mars Base). Choosing an environment changes the distance to Earth and the communication delay. A holographic body shows the status of each region; clicking a region opens its indicators, the two-axis display, charts over time and short explanations in plain language, because we assume the astronaut is not a medical expert. A demo mode shows a simple fixed-threshold monitor next to SERENA on the same data, so the difference can be seen in a few seconds.

The five spaceflight hazards (NASA HRP)

  • Space radiation: an accumulated-dose indicator based on real NASA OSDR/RadLab dose data (lunar orbit, Mars surface, BioSentinel).
  • Isolation and confinement: mood and sleep check-ins as part of the daily routine.
  • Distance from Earth: everything runs onboard and offline, with a visible communication delay and three escalation levels.
  • Gravity fields: detection of gradual cardiovascular deconditioning and reminders for exercise countermeasures.
  • Hostile closed environment: cabin CO2 (ISSLIVE data and NASA references) checked against respiration.

Use of AI in the system

AI does not decide whether data can be trusted and cannot silence an alarm. All verification is deterministic: the core makes no LLM calls, uses no network and has no unseeded randomness, and an architecture test enforces this. AI is only used around Layer 0. Deterministic red-team attacks are used to test the checks in the benchmark, and an optional explainer (future work) would describe a verdict using only its own evidence. We follow a Simplex safety pattern, so no AI component can change, silence or downgrade a Layer 0 alarm. When there is doubt, SERENA alerts, so a possible real event is never hidden because it might be an attack.

Results

We ran an ablation on held-out test data, comparing Layer 0 off and on:

  • Safety: 0 of 121 labelled real-event windows were suppressed. This was our main priority.
  • PPG-DaLiA: with Layer 0 off, 100% of attacked windows pass as verified. With Layer 0 on, this drops to 26.5%, and all 70 attack cases are detected (72.0% of eligible attacked windows, median time to detection 10 s).
  • IoMT-SecAlarmBench: attacked windows passing as verified drop from 100% to 7.6%, with 96 of 151 cases detected and a median time to detection of about 4 s.

These are raw results with 95% confidence intervals and documented limitations. The whole benchmark can be regenerated with one command.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend (Python 3.12): FastAPI with WebSocket, NumPy, SciPy, NeuroKit2 for physiological signal processing, RTAMT for signal temporal logic, PyNaCl for Ed25519 signatures, pgmpy for probabilistic attribution, a hash-chained signed ledger in SQLite, and LangGraph for the optional agent layer.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript and three.js for the 3D ship and body, with GSAP and Lenis for animation. It runs fully offline.
  • Benchmark: a reproducible ablation setup with fixed seeds, confidence intervals and a results table.

Design decisions

Most health monitors show a number. We wanted SERENA to also show whether that number can be believed, and to make that easy to see quickly. The main factors we considered were autonomy (it works without a link to Earth), transparency (unverifiable data is shown as Unknown, not hidden or filled in), reproducibility (public datasets, cited sources and a benchmark anyone can run) and clarity for a non-expert under stress. Any synthetic or mock data is labelled in the interface, and every clinical range is taken from a NASA standard or a named clinical source.

Expected impact

A tool that astronauts can rely on when they have to make health decisions alone, far from Earth. It should reduce both false alarms that lead to unnecessary action and real events that go unnoticed, and it gives flight surgeons a verifiable record when the crew does escalate.

Limitations and future work

SERENA is not a certified medical device and does not diagnose or prescribe. We could not find open time-series of human physiological data from spaceflight in OSDR, so physiological validation uses terrestrial datasets (PPG-DaLiA and IoMT-SecAlarmBench), while radiation and environment data come from NASA OSDR. The false-positive rate on the clinical alert path is currently high (raw rates, no conformal bound yet). This comes from our choice to alert when in doubt, and we plan to reduce it. Accuracy in telling sensor faults apart from attacks is still below our target. Next steps include immune and bone markers from NASA OSDR as a research extension and an LLM explainer with a deterministic audit.
